items.title: Campbell Price On The Rise Of Ramesses II
items.description:
The name of Ramesses the Great is etched deeper into Egypt than almost any other ruler.  Colossal statues moulded in his image tower over the Nile. Reliefs of his victories are carved into countless temple walls. But where did Ramesses II come from? And how was this legend of Egyptian history born?

In this episode of The Ancients, Tristan Hughes is joined by Dr Campbell Price to uncover the rise of the House of Ramesses and the century of crisis that paved the way for Egypt’s most famous pharao

items.title: Medieval Employment | The Best & Worst Jobs at the Tower in the 1200s
items.description: The Tower of London underwent significant change during the 1200s under the medieval kings, Henry III and Edward I. But the Tower wasn’t just home to knights and royals. Life in the medieval palace was only possible because of hundreds of servants who lived with king and queen, and followed the court wherever it went. global_silver_linings.title: Did Scientists Just Detect the First Known ‘Exomoon’?
global_silver_linings.snippet: As soon as Aleksander Wolszczan confirmed the observation of the first planet outside of our solar system, he immediately reasoned that thousands more would be discovered in the coming decades. On that prediction the astronomer, now 80, was eminently correct, and the trend has expanded to the point that recent observation seems to include the […] The post Did Scientists Just Detect the First Known ‘Exomoon’? appeared first on Good News Network .
global_silver_linings.reason: If confirmed, the discovery of the first moon orbiting a planet beyond our solar system would mean we are no longer alone in having the kind of cosmic neighbourhoods that nurture complex worlds. It's a reminder that the universe is far richer and stranger than we can yet imagine.

global_silver_linings.title: Leopards recover in Zambia as communities swap skins for synthetics
global_silver_linings.snippet: Replacing real leopard skins with synthetic furs has helped leopards recover in western Zambia, researchers say The post Leopards recover in Zambia as communities swap skins for synthetics appeared first on Positive News .
global_silver_linings.reason: Leopard populations in Zambia are genuinely rebounding after local communities chose synthetic alternatives to wild animal skins — proof that when conservation works with people rather than against them, nature gets a real chance to recover.

global_silver_linings.title: Unearthing Paris’ Mythical Second River
global_silver_linings.snippet: Only knee-deep in parts yet relatively wide, the Bièvre gently flows with transparent waters that shimmer in the afternoon sun. A shoal of fish lazily linger beside a large stone in one section. Further along, birds and butterflies weave between the long grasses lining the banks.
global_silver_linings.reason: Beneath the streets of Paris lies a long-forgotten river quietly waiting to be rediscovered, and the effort to unearth it speaks to a growing movement to bring nature back into the heart of our cities. Restoring hidden waterways can cool urban heat, support wildlife, and reconnect communities with the living landscape beneath their feet.

discovery_articles.title: The Big Kangaroo (Rooey II) in Nullarbor, Australia
discovery_articles.snippet: Towering high beside the Border Village Roadhouse, situated on the edge of the Nullarbor Plain is Rooey II. This large kangaroo sculpture is one of many 'Big Things', found around Australia as something of an unofficial national tradition. Rooey II sits in South Australia, only metres away from the Western Australia border.

discovery_articles.title: Submarine Safari in Amarilla Golf, Spain
discovery_articles.snippet: Tenerife is a versatile island with beautiful nature, lively party locations, state-of-the-art telescopes, and amazing beaches. Most tourists stay on land or close to it, some go off shore to watch whales or dolphins, but unbeknownst to most some also go under the sea in a submarine. Submarine safari is a local company running one of the few submarines open to the public.

featured_read.title: Do the Next Right Thing: Carl Jung on How to Live and the Origin of His Famous Tenet for Navigating Uncertainty
featured_read.snippet: "There is no pit you cannot climb out of provided you make the right effort at the right place... do the next thing with diligence and devotion."
featured_read.blurb: Jung's deceptively simple instruction — do the next right thing — turns out to be a complete philosophy for surviving the moments when the full path is invisible. This essay traces how he arrived at it, and why it holds.

garden_note.note: High summer has Zürich glowing at its most abundant tonight — the kitchen garden is thick with courgettes that seem to double in size between breakfast and supper, and the linden trees that gave the city its name have finished flowering but left the warm air with the faintest honeyed memory. Step outside after the sun slips away at 21:08 and let the evening do its slow, golden work.
